title: Option Pricing using Quantum Computers
abstract_summary: The paper presents a methodology to price vanilla, multi-asset and path-dependent options on gate-based quantum computers using Amplitude Estimation, which offers a theoretical quadratic speedup over classical Monte Carlo. It emphasizes concrete quantum-circuit constructions to load probability distributions, compute payoffs, and perform amplitude estimation, provides simulation results, and demonstrates small-scale experiments on IBM Q Tokyo using an error-mitigation scheme and amplitude estimation without phase estimation.
methodology_description: The authors propose and implement a gate-based quantum approach to option pricing that leverages Amplitude Estimation (AE) to compute expected payoffs (undiscounted) with a theoretical quadratic speedup versus classical Monte Carlo. Their pipeline: (1) represent the future distribution of underlying asset prices on quantum registers (truncation + discretization of log-normal BSM distributions; for general/market-implied distributions they discuss using qGANs to load learned distributions), (2) implement payoff circuits using controlled Y-rotations and comparator circuits to realize piecewise-linear payoffs (vanilla calls/puts, multi-strike portfolios, basket options, Asian and barrier options), (3) construct operator A that prepares the amplitude-encoded probability & payoff ancilla, (4) apply amplitude-estimation techniques to estimate the ancilla |1> amplitude which equals the expectation value of the payoff. They evaluate both the standard AE that includes phase estimation (in simulation) and a reduced-qubit AE variant without phase estimation (per Suzuki et al.) that uses repeated applications of Q^k and a maximum-likelihood estimator to recover the amplitude (used on real hardware). Implementation details include adder/weighted-sum circuits for multi-asset and path-dependent payoffs, comparator circuits implemented with CNOT/Toffoli gates, scaling/angle transforms to map payoffs into rotation angles for the ancilla, and practical error mitigation: readout calibration matrices and a CNOT-amplification + Richardson-extrapolation style mitigation (by replacing each CNOT with 1/3/5 CNOTs to amplify noise, then quadratic extrapolation to zero-noise). Experiments were run in simulation (Qiskit) and on IBM Quantum hardware (IBM Q Tokyo). Results compare AE convergence to classical Monte Carlo baselines and demonstrate hardware feasibility of small instances using AE without QPE combined with mitigation and maximum-likelihood estimation.

experimental_setup: Simulations: Qiskit-based simulations of amplitude estimation including standard AE (with sampling qubits m = 3,5,7,9 corresponding to M = 8,32,128,512). Classical Monte Carlo baselines (up to 100,000 paths for some cases) used for comparison. Hardware experiments: IBM Q Tokyo (20-qubit device). Hardware experiments used a 3-qubit implementation (2 qubits for discretized uncertainty, 1 ancilla payoff qubit). For AE-without-QPE they implemented QA^k for k=0,1 (i.e. m=1), measured repeated shots and applied maximum-likelihood estimation. Error mitigation: readout calibration (8x8 matrix for 3 qubits) and CNOT-amplification (replace each CNOT by 1, 3, and 5 CNOTs) followed by second-order Richardson extrapolation. Hardware measurement protocol: 8192 shots per run, each experiment repeated 20 times and averaged. Qubit choices on device: qubits 6, 10 and 11 (fully connected subset).
dataset_used: No external market dataset. All experiments used simulated asset-price distributions derived from the Black-Scholes-Merton model (log-normal distributions). Distributions were truncated to a finite interval and discretized into 2^n bins (e.g., 2 qubits → 4 bins). For multi-step/path-dependent options the multivariate log-normal distribution (diagonal Σ for independent timesteps or full Σ for correlated assets) was used. qGANs are discussed as a method to load empirical/market-implied distributions but hardware experiments used simulated BSM distributions.
experiment_input: Source: simulated Black-Scholes-Merton (BSM) log-normal asset-price distributions (single-asset and multivariate for multi-asset/path-dependent cases). Typical parameters given in examples: S0 (spot) varied (hardware experiments used S0 in [1.8,2.5] stepping by 0.1), volatility σ (example: 40% in hardware tests), risk-free rate r (example: 5%), time to maturity T (example: 40/365). Discretization: truncation to ±~3 standard deviations, mapping continuous price interval to integer indices i ∈ {0,..,2^n −1} via affine mapping. For hardware experiments n=2 uncertainty qubits (4 discrete price bins). Payoff scaling: linear mapping and angle scaling parameter c (example c=0.25) used to map payoffs into rotation angles for ancilla. No external real-world dataset used.
experiment_process: 1) Distribution preparation: compute discretized/truncated log-normal probabilities for the chosen BSM parameters and map to amplitudes; for general distributions qGAN is proposed to learn and output a parametrized generator circuit. 2) State loading: implement PX to load √p_i amplitudes into the n-qubit register (hardware: 2-qubit approximation of log-normal using single-qubit rotations + CNOTs). 3) Payoff encoding: construct comparator circuits (CNOT/Toffoli) to identify regions (i ≥ K), and implement controlled Y-rotations (uniformly-controlled rotations for small instances) to map payoff f(i) into ancilla amplitude (angles computed via scaling c and linear mapping). 4) AE operator construction: build A such that measuring ancilla |1> yields E[f(S)]; build Q = A S0 A† Sψ0. For full AE (simulation) apply Q controlled by m sampling qubits and inverse QFT to estimate phase (m varied). For AE without phase estimation (hardware) perform measurement of Q^k A |0> for k = 0..(2^m −1) as per Suzuki et al. with m=1 in hardware experiments (k=0,1). 5) Measurement & estimation: measure circuits (8192 shots per run), collect probabilities for ancilla |1>, combine outcomes across k in a likelihood function and apply maximum-likelihood estimation to extract θ_a and amplitude a = sin^2(θ_a). 6) Error mitigation: apply readout-error mitigation by constructing and inverting an 8×8 readout matrix; amplify CNOT error by replacing each CNOT with 1, 3, and 5 CNOT sequences (no recalibration) and perform second-order Richardson extrapolation (quadratic fit) to estimate zero-noise value. 7) Postprocessing: map measured amplitude back to expected payoff using known scaling parameters (fmin/fmax/c) and compare to analytical Black-Scholes or classical Monte Carlo baselines. Repeats: each hardware experiment repeated 20 times and averaged. Simulation variants: full AE with m ∈ {3,5,7,9} to evaluate convergence.

results_summary: The paper presents a detailed methodology and gate-level circuits to price a variety of option types (vanilla European, multi-asset basket, path-dependent Asian and barrier options) on gate-based quantum computers using Amplitude Estimation (AE). It describes how to load distributions (including a discussion of qGAN-based loading), construct payoff encodings (comparators, piecewise-linear rotations), and compute multivariate sums (adder/weighted-sum circuits). Simulations validate AE's improved sample-complexity scaling versus classical Monte Carlo for toy examples. The authors also run small-scale experiments on IBM Q Tokyo (3 qubits) using an AE variant without phase estimation, and demonstrate that readout calibration plus an error-amplification + Richardson-extrapolation mitigation reduces hardware estimation error substantially (reported average error drop from ~62% to ~21%). The work provides concrete resource estimates showing that full AE circuits become deep and gate-intensive quickly, indicating that practical, large-scale quantum advantage will require more advanced hardware.

quantum_advantage_detail: The paper argues (and cites proofs) that Amplitude Estimation provides a quadratic sample-complexity speed-up over classical Monte Carlo (O(M^-1) vs O(M^-1/2)), and simulation results on toy examples support improved scaling. However, no empirical demonstration of a practical advantage on real quantum hardware is presented — hardware experiments are limited to very small (3-qubit) circuits and show substantial noise that required mitigation. The authors therefore frame the advantage as theoretically established and observed in simulation, but contingent on future larger, lower-noise or fault-tolerant devices for practical realization.
